# Table of Contents

The on-this-page nav beside a long document. It marks the section being read as you scroll, with a bar that slides along a hairline track, and it needs nothing but the links themselves.

```tsx
const pane = React.useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null)

<div ref={pane} className="h-90 overflow-y-auto">
  <article>
    <h3 id="brief">The brief</h3>
    …
  </article>
</div>

<TableOfContents container={pane} defaultValue="brief">
  <TableOfContentsTitle>On this page</TableOfContentsTitle>
  <TableOfContentsList>
    <TableOfContentsItem href="#brief">The brief</TableOfContentsItem>
    <TableOfContentsItem href="#constraints">Constraints first</TableOfContentsItem>
    <TableOfContentsItem href="#signals">Signals over strings</TableOfContentsItem>
    <TableOfContentsItem href="#ranking">Ranking, not filtering</TableOfContentsItem>
    <TableOfContentsItem href="#shipping">Shipping it fast</TableOfContentsItem>
  </TableOfContentsList>
</TableOfContents>
```

## Installation

```bash
# One-time setup (tokens + lib helpers)
npx koalaui-cli@latest init

# Add this component (its dependencies come along)
npx koalaui-cli@latest add table-of-contents
```

Manual: run `npm install radix-ui tailwind-variants tailwind-merge`, then copy the source into `components/ui/table-of-contents/` and adjust the import paths to your project. Components pull `cn` from `lib/utils`, the `tv` wrapper from `lib/tv`, and (for multi-part components) `createContext` from `lib/create-context`.

## Usage

```tsx title="usage.tsx"
import {
  TableOfContents,
  TableOfContentsTitle,
  TableOfContentsList,
  TableOfContentsItem,
} from "@/components/ui/table-of-contents"

<aside className="hidden lg:block">
  <TableOfContents className="sticky top-24">
    <TableOfContentsTitle>On this page</TableOfContentsTitle>
    <TableOfContentsList>
      {sections.map((section) => (
        <TableOfContentsItem key={section.id} href={`#${section.id}`}>
          {section.title}
        </TableOfContentsItem>
      ))}
    </TableOfContentsList>
  </TableOfContents>
</aside>
```

There is no list of ids to keep in step: each item registers the heading its `href` points at, and the nav watches those headings. Pin the rail yourself (`sticky` under your header) and give the headings a `scroll-margin-top` that clears that header, which the spy reads too. The items are plain anchors, so the jump, the URL hash and the back button stay the browser's; for a glide, set `scroll-behavior: smooth` on `html` behind `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference`.

## Variants

Six looks over one behaviour, so switching is a prop, never a rewrite. Line is the default: a hairline track with a brand bar that slides to the section being read. Progress fills the same track from the top down to that section, so it also says how far in the reader is. Pill slides a soft chip behind the active row, the Sidebar's active fill, for a rail inside an app. Dash leads every row with a short rule that runs to full length on the active one. Plain marks it by ink and weight alone. Minimap rests as a column of dashes and opens into the list; it has its own section below. Click an item to move the mark.

```tsx
<TableOfContents>…</TableOfContents>                    {/* line (default) */}
<TableOfContents variant="progress">…</TableOfContents>
<TableOfContents variant="pill">…</TableOfContents>
<TableOfContents variant="dash">…</TableOfContents>
<TableOfContents variant="plain">…</TableOfContents>
<TableOfContents variant="minimap">…</TableOfContents>
```

## Minimap

The quietest rail: a column of dashes hung from the page's edge, one per section, subsections shorter, the one being read longer and in brand. It shows the shape of the document without a word of text. Hover it, or Tab into it, and the menu surface grows out of the column into the full list, clipped from its corner so the dashes swell into the panel instead of a popover appearing beside them. A mouse click on a link lets it close as soon as the pointer leaves; keyboard focus holds it open. The panel opens toward the content, so give the rail a column at the edge of the page.

```tsx
<div className="grid grid-cols-[minmax(0,1fr)_auto] gap-6">
  <article>…</article>
  <TableOfContents variant="minimap" className="sticky top-24 self-start">
    <TableOfContentsTitle>On this page</TableOfContentsTitle>
    <TableOfContentsList>
      <TableOfContentsItem href="#brief">The brief</TableOfContentsItem>
      …
    </TableOfContentsList>
  </TableOfContents>
</div>
```

## Levels

`level={3}` makes an item a subsection: it steps in 16px under its parent, and on the line variant the bar still runs down the same track, so the mark never jumps sideways between a section and its children. Two levels is the limit on purpose: a third reads as a sitemap, not a guide to the page.

```tsx
<TableOfContentsList>
  <TableOfContentsItem href="#requirements">Requirements</TableOfContentsItem>
  <TableOfContentsItem href="#install">Install</TableOfContentsItem>
  <TableOfContentsItem href="#cli" level={3}>With the CLI</TableOfContentsItem>
  <TableOfContentsItem href="#manual" level={3}>By hand</TableOfContentsItem>
  <TableOfContentsItem href="#configure">Configure</TableOfContentsItem>
  <TableOfContentsItem href="#tokens" level={3}>Tokens</TableOfContentsItem>
  <TableOfContentsItem href="#density" level={3}>Density</TableOfContentsItem>
  <TableOfContentsItem href="#next">Next steps</TableOfContentsItem>
</TableOfContentsList>
```

## Numbered

`numbered` prefixes each item with its position, for a document people cite by clause: a policy, terms, a spec. The numbers are CSS counters on the list, so they always agree with the order on screen, and a level-3 item reads `2.1` under its parent. Screen readers already get the order from the `<ol>`, so the glyphs are hidden from them.

```tsx
<TableOfContents numbered>
  <TableOfContentsTitle>Privacy policy</TableOfContentsTitle>
  <TableOfContentsList>
    <TableOfContentsItem href="#collect">What we collect</TableOfContentsItem>
    <TableOfContentsItem href="#use">How we use it</TableOfContentsItem>
    <TableOfContentsItem href="#billing" level={3}>Receipts and billing</TableOfContentsItem>
    <TableOfContentsItem href="#releases" level={3}>Release notes</TableOfContentsItem>
    <TableOfContentsItem href="#share">Who we share it with</TableOfContentsItem>
    <TableOfContentsItem href="#cookies">Cookies</TableOfContentsItem>
    <TableOfContentsItem href="#rights">Your rights</TableOfContentsItem>
  </TableOfContentsList>
</TableOfContents>
```

## Density

Compact rows are 32px, the Sidebar's, for a docs rail that has to fit a long page. Comfortable rows reach the 40px house minimum, so the whole row is an easy target on a marketing page. On a touch screen both grow to 44px: the row itself grows, since stacked rows can't borrow space from each other. Without the prop it follows the nearest `DensityProvider`, and compact when there is none.

```tsx
<TableOfContents density="compact">…</TableOfContents>
<TableOfContents density="comfortable">…</TableOfContents>
```

## Headings from the page

`useHeadings(selector)` reads the headings out of the DOM, so a docs or blog layout builds its items from whatever the page renders. Levels are relative: the shallowest heading found is a section and anything deeper a subsection, so an article built from `h3`s nests the same as one built from `h2`s. Controls inside a heading (a copy-link anchor) are left out of its label. In a layout that persists across routes, pass the pathname as the second argument to read them again.

```tsx
const headings = useHeadings("article :is(h3, h4)[id]")

<TableOfContents container={pane}>
  <TableOfContentsTitle>On this page</TableOfContentsTitle>
  <TableOfContentsList>
    {headings.map((heading) => (
      <TableOfContentsItem key={heading.id} href={`#${heading.id}`} level={heading.level}>
        {heading.text}
      </TableOfContentsItem>
    ))}
  </TableOfContentsList>
</TableOfContents>
```

## How the spy decides

- A heading counts as reached once it sits where an anchor jump would park it: the top of the view plus its own `scroll-margin-top`. The spy reads the margin off the heading, so it agrees with the jump under a sticky header without a second offset.
- The first heading not yet reached is the section being read if it is already in the top half of the view; lower down, the reader is still in the one before it.
- At the very end of a page that scrolled, the last section wins, since the closing sections are often too short to ever reach the top.
- A clicked item holds the mark while the page travels to it, so a smooth scroll doesn't flick through every section on the way, and hands it back as soon as the reader scrolls themselves.
- `container` watches a scroll pane instead of the window (every demo on this page does). There, an item scrolls the pane itself, since a native jump would move the page around it too.
- A rail that scrolls on its own, capped at the viewport height like the one beside this page, keeps the active item in view as the mark moves. Only the rail scrolls, never the page.

## Reacting to the section

`onValueChange` hears the id of the section being read, from the spy or a click: update a reading bar, the document title, an analytics event. Pass `value` to drive the mark yourself, and `defaultValue` so the server render already marks the first section instead of waiting for the spy's first reading.

```tsx
const [reading, setReading] = React.useState("The brief")

<p>Reading {reading}</p>

<TableOfContents
  container={pane}
  defaultValue="brief"
  onValueChange={(id) => setReading(titles[id])}
>
  …
</TableOfContents>
```

## A nav of your own

`useScrollSpy(ids)` is the same spy without the list, for when a rail doesn't fit: a phone that shows the section being read in a bar instead. It starts on the first id, so the server render already has an answer. Here the headings carry `scroll-mt-12` to clear the bar, and the spy honors it.

```tsx
const active = useScrollSpy(["brief", "constraints", "signals", "ranking", "shipping"], {
  container: pane,
})

<div ref={pane} className="h-90 overflow-y-auto">
  <div className="sticky top-0 flex h-10 items-center justify-between border-b bg-background">
    <span className="truncate font-medium">{titles[active]}</span>
    <span className="tabular-nums text-muted-foreground">{index + 1} / 5</span>
  </div>
  <article className="[&_h3]:scroll-mt-12">…</article>
</div>
```

## API reference

### TableOfContents

The `<nav>` and the spy. Takes `variant` (line · progress · pill · dash · plain · minimap), `density` (compact · comfortable), `numbered`, `value`, `defaultValue`, `onValueChange` and `container` (a ref to a scroll pane; the window when omitted). Its `aria-label` defaults to `"On this page"`; give each nav its own when a page has two.

### TableOfContentsTitle

The overline above the list, a `<p>`. `asChild` renders your own element instead, such as a heading.

### TableOfContentsList

The `<ol>`. On line and progress it draws the track and the bar, on pill the chip, each its own `::before`, so `className="before:bg-foreground"` restyles it. On minimap the list is the panel, and the dash column renders beside it from the same items.

### TableOfContentsItem

One link in its `<li>`. Takes `href` (`#` plus the heading's id; a link that leaves the page is shown but not spied) and `level` (2 · 3). The active item carries `aria-current="location"`.

### useHeadings · useScrollSpy

`useHeadings(selector?, key?)` returns `{ id, text, level }[]` for the headings matching `selector` (default `"h2[id], h3[id]"`), read again when `key` changes. `useScrollSpy(ids, { container? })` returns the id of the section being read.

## FAQ

### Why doesn't it take a list of ids?

Because the items already say where they point. Each TableOfContentsItem registers the heading its href names, so the spy always watches exactly the links on screen, and adding or removing an item needs no second edit elsewhere.

### Why aren't the clicks smooth?

The items are plain anchors, so the browser owns the jump, the hash in the URL, the back button and where Tab goes next. Add scroll-behavior: smooth to html inside @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) and every anchor on the site glides, this one included. The mark doesn't wait for the scroll: it moves to the clicked item at once.

### The wrong section lights up under my sticky header. What do I change?

Give the headings a scroll-margin-top that clears the header (scroll-mt-24 under a 64px bar, say). The anchor jump parks the heading below the header, and the spy reads the same margin to decide when a heading has been reached, so the two agree.

### Where does a share row or a back-to-top link go?

Beside the nav, not inside it: wrap both in a column and let the TableOfContents stay navigation only. That is how the Blog Post 2 page composes its rail.

### What should a phone show?

A rail rarely fits below lg. Hide it there and either put the same list above the article as a plain index, the way the Legal Section 2 section does, or show the section being read in a bar with useScrollSpy.

### Does it respect reduced motion?

Yes. The bar jumps instead of sliding, and inside a scroll container a click scrolls instantly. The page itself scrolls however your html rule says.

## Exports and dependencies

`npx koalaui-cli@latest add table-of-contents` writes `components/ui/table-of-contents/`. Import from `@/components/ui/table-of-contents`:

- Components and helpers: `TableOfContents`, `TableOfContentsTitle`, `TableOfContentsList`, `TableOfContentsItem`, `useScrollSpy`, `useHeadings`, `tableOfContentsVariants`
- Types: `TableOfContentsProps`, `TableOfContentsTitleProps`, `TableOfContentsItemProps`, `TableOfContentsHeading`, `TableOfContentsLevel`, `UseScrollSpyOptions`
- Koala lib helpers it uses: `create-context`, `density`, `tv`
- npm packages: `radix-ui`
